title: Mitomycin + fluorouracil with radiotherapy
purpose: Support radiotherapy in treating bladder cancer while aiming to preserve the bladder in selected patients.
schedule_label: Mitomycin day 1 · five-day pumps on days 1–5 and 22–26
schedule_summary: Mitomycin is given once on day 1. Fluorouracil runs continuously through a pump over 120 hours on days 1–5 and again on days 22–26, alongside the prescribed radiotherapy course. This is one chemoradiation course, not a repeating 28-day chemotherapy cycle.
administration_text: Mitomycin is given through a carefully checked intravenous line. Each fluorouracil pump provides 500 mg/m² per day for five days, a total of 2500 mg/m² over 120 hours. The unit arranges pump connection, disconnection and line care.

agents.name: Mitomycin
agents.mechanism: Links DNA strands so cells cannot copy them normally
agents.explanation: Mitomycin damages the DNA that dividing cells need. With fluorouracil it helps radiotherapy act against bladder cancer. Healthy marrow and other tissues can also be affected.
agents.watch: Report fever, unusual bruising, reduced urine, breathlessness or pain around the drip promptly.
risks: Low blood counts, serious infection and bleeding, which may be delayed
Nausea, mouth soreness and skin reactions
Tissue damage if the medicine leaks outside the vein
Rare serious kidney/blood-vessel injury including haemolytic uraemic syndrome
Rare serious lung inflammation; possible fertility harm

agents.name: Fluorouracil
agents.mechanism: Disrupts production of DNA and RNA
agents.explanation: Fluorouracil, often shortened to 5-FU, interferes with the building blocks used to make DNA and RNA, which cells need to grow. It runs through a vein over the prescribed hours. Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) is an enzyme that breaks it down. Testing for DPD deficiency before treatment reduces risk but cannot rule out every severe reaction.
agents.watch: Report severe diarrhoea, mouth sores, chest pain, sudden confusion, sore palms or soles, or unexpectedly early severe symptoms.
risks: Low blood counts and serious infection
Rare severe neurological or early excessive toxicity

anatomy: New breathlessness or cough needs urgent assessment.
Report painful mouth ulcers, especially if you cannot drink.
Chest pain, breathlessness or faintness needs emergency assessment.
Report diarrhoea early; severe pain or dehydration needs urgent help.
Report reduced urine, blood in urine or painful urination.
Fever, sudden illness or unusual bleeding needs urgent advice.
Report painful palms/soles, rash or pain/swelling around the intravenous line.
Sudden confusion, unsteadiness or severe unexpected symptoms need urgent help.

evidence.title: BC2001 · 2012 and ten-year follow-up
evidence.summary: In BC2001, 360 people were randomised to bladder radiotherapy with or without fluorouracil and mitomycin. Two-year freedom from locoregional disease was 67% with chemoradiation versus 54% with radiotherapy alone (hazard ratio 0.68, 95% confidence interval 0.48–0.96).
evidence.intro: In BC2001, 360 people were randomised to bladder radiotherapy with or without fluorouracil and mitomycin. Two-year freedom from locoregional disease was 67% with chemoradiation versus 54% with radiotherapy alone (hazard ratio 0.68, 95% confidence interval 0.48–0.96).
evidence.caveat: This demonstrates improved local control compared with radiotherapy alone; it does not prove superiority to bladder-removal surgery. Overall survival was not significantly different in the primary report. Suitability for bladder preservation requires multidisciplinary assessment.
evidence.interpretation: This demonstrates improved local control compared with radiotherapy alone; it does not prove superiority to bladder-removal surgery. questions.q: What is the treatment trying to do?
questions.a: Support radiotherapy in treating bladder cancer while aiming to preserve the bladder in selected patients. Radiotherapy treats the bladder locally while chemotherapy makes cancer cells more sensitive to it. The radiation oncology team specifies dose, fractions and preparation. Follow-up bladder examinations are essential, and surgery may still be required if treatment does not control the cancer.

Mitomycin is given once on day 1. Fluorouracil runs continuously through a pump over 120 hours on days 1–5 and again on days 22–26, alongside the prescribed radiotherapy course. This is one chemoradiation course, not a repeating 28-day chemotherapy cycle.

questions.q: Does a delay mean treatment has failed?
questions.a: No. Blood counts, organ function and symptoms can make a delay or dose change safer. Your team decides whether and when to give the next dose.

questions.q: Who do I contact if unwell?
questions.a: Use your verified oncology daytime or out-of-hours number. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Severe symptoms require 112/999.

Trained staff connect a prescribed 120-hour fluorouracil infusion on each scheduled start day.
Each pump runs for 120 hours. Carry it as shown; never change the settings yourself.
The team confirms the exact disconnection time from the actual connection time. Keep the appointment even if the pump appears empty.
Pump disconnection does not remove a port or PICC. Agree ongoing line care and any separate removal appointment.
